clue.text: Learned dons robbed — odd items taken out and trashed

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the shortened word wears the synonym for learned inside it
the first, third and fifth letters of robbed are dropped, leaving the even ones

parts.note: learned, as in well read, means literate

explanation.surface: Scholarly university dons have been burgled, with some strange things taken and the place wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned dons' reads as academics, but 'dons' is a verb meaning puts on, so the shortened 'robbed' goes around the synonym for learned.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obliterated has been wiped out or destroyed, just as a trashed thing is wrecked.

clue.text: Gentle saint overlooked time and again in literature

indicators.note: a thing overlooked is missed out, so the abbreviation for saint is left out of the word

parts.note: gentle means soft

explanation.surface: A mild holy person repeatedly ignored in books.
explanation.definitionFit: Oft is the old poetic form of often, a word for repeatedly found mostly in older writing.

clue.text: Nomads decline to use speech

indicators.note: speaking the word aloud signals that the answer is a soundalike

parts.note: to decline is to lapse, to slip into a worse state

explanation.surface: Wandering people refuse to talk.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sami of northern Scandinavia, once called by this name, were traditionally reindeer-herding wanderers.

clue.text: What hiker did to go back across motorway

indicators.note: the reversed word is laid across, enclosing, the motorway letter
back says the synonym for go is read in reverse

parts.note: to go is to depart
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the British M1

explanation.surface: A walker's journey involved turning round and crossing a big road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go back' reads like a single phrase but 'back' turns DEPART into TRAPED, and M goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiker walks a long way on foot, which is what tramping means.

clue.text: Break up once, never to get together again

indicators.note: breaking the words up means their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A couple split once and vow never to reunite.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about lovers, but 'get together again' is the definition, the opposite of what the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To reconvene is for a meeting or group to assemble once more after a pause.

clue.text: Pound's writing poetically from start to finish of book

parts.words: writing poetically from start to finish
parts.note: thro is the poetic spelling of through, meaning from start to finish

explanation.surface: The poet Ezra Pound writes verse from the first page to the last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like the poet's name; it is the definition, a verb meaning beat.
explanation.definitionFit: To pound and to throb are both to beat heavily and rhythmically, as a headache does.

clue.text: Waste a long time in prison cell

parts.note: dung is animal waste
an eon is an immensely long period

explanation.surface: Wasting years locked up in a jail cell.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is an underground cell where prisoners were kept, usually in a castle.

clue.text: Where to keep milk cooler

definitions.meaning: a pitcher or similar vessel holding milk

explanation.definitionFit: A jug holds milk for the table, and jug is also old slang for a jail, as cooler is.

clue.text: Fold flag, badly cut

parts.note: a jack is a flag flown on a ship, as in Union Jack
to knife someone is to wound them by cutting

explanation.surface: Fold up a flag that has been clumsily trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: To jackknife is to fold up sharply in the middle, like a lorry skidding or a diver bending.

clue.text: Huntin' shootin' and fishin' bore, one described by novelist

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so the novelist's name goes around the other pieces

parts.note: Graham Greene was an English novelist
a bore is a hole drilled for water, a well
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A tedious country-sports type is portrayed by a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' reads as a tedious person in the surface; it is a well. Green wellies, rubber boots, are the badge of Britain's country-sports set.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used for the rural upper-class set devoted to field sports, known by their green rubber boots.

clue.text: Entertainer needing floorboards and carpet replaced

indicators.note: the letters are put back in a different order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A performer requires a new floor and new carpeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'floorboards' seems part of a home-improvement list; it belongs to the definition, since this performer needs a hard floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tap performer needs a hard wooden surface for the metal plates on the shoes to click on.

clue.text: Recess set back in church (Eastern)

indicators.note: set back says the little word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A recess positioned further back inside an Orthodox church.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a shallow recess in a wall, often holding a statue.

clue.text: Stand up, shattering part of housemaid's kit

indicators.note: shattering breaks the words into pieces to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Getting to one's feet, a maid breaks some of the cleaning gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A housemaid sweeps dirt into this flat scoop with a brush.

clue.text: The best of students pines to be seen in Tudor garb

indicators.note: the trees are seen inside the garment

parts.note: a doublet is the close-fitting jacket worn by men in Tudor times
pines are firs, both conifers

explanation.surface: Top students yearn to appear in sixteenth-century costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pines' looks like a verb meaning yearns; it is the trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A double first is a first-class degree in two subjects at a British university, the highest result.

clue.text: Domesticate the family, money being short at first

indicators.note: the money comes first, before the family
short means missing its final letter

parts.note: bread is slang for money
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: Taming the household when funds are low at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: To break in a horse is to tame and train it for use.

clue.text: Pay Union leader for spades to make stand

indicators.note: the union's first letter stands in for the abbreviation for spades

parts.note: to pay out is to spend
S is the abbreviation for spades in card games

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: The union boss pays for shovels to make a strike stand.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend something is to set it on its end, making it stand upright.

clue.text: Chef frequently uses this chopper

definitions.meaning: a kitchen whisk for beating eggs

explanation.definitionFit: The kitchen whisk is the cook's tool, and the same name is American slang for a helicopter, whose rotors whirl like one.

clue.text: Rose like industrious worker breaking rank

parts.note: eg, for example, introduces something like what was said

indicators.note: the worker breaks into the row, splitting it

parts.note: a rank is a line, as of soldiers
the ant is proverbially hard-working

explanation.surface: Rising, like a diligent employee leaving the ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' reads as a verb; it is the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweetbriar, a wild flower of the rose family.

clue.text: Carry on with abandon — resistance ends here

parts.note: to last is to carry on or endure
to ditch is to abandon

explanation.surface: Keep going recklessly, since opposition stops at this point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with abandon' looks like a phrase meaning recklessly; 'abandon' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: The final trench defenders hold before defeat gives its name to a desperate final effort.

clue.text: Set fire to homes, with no time for delicacy

parts.note: to light is to set fire to

indicators.note: with no time means the abbreviation for time is removed

parts.note: nests are birds' homes

explanation.surface: An arsonist torches houses, with no time for finesse.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicacy of touch is gentleness, the quality of being light rather than heavy.

clue.text: Work finally completed in borough under central control

indicators.note: the pieces sit in the town

parts.note: a borough is a town
op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A project finally finished in a council area under government direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A top-down system is run by orders from the centre rather than from below.

clue.text: First-class biographer's book — nothing removed

indicators.note: removed says those letters are taken out of the name

parts.note: James Boswell wrote the life of Samuel Johnson
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A top-quality life story, published uncut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing removed' reads as uncut; it is O, taken out with B.
explanation.definitionFit: Swell is dated slang for excellent, first-rate.

clue.text: Class sees problem cutting up blocks

indicators.note: the problem holds the turned word inside it, as a block holds back

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a cutting remark is tart, sharp

explanation.surface: A class watches a tricky exercise in chopping up wooden blocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting up' looks like a phrase for chopping; 'cutting' is TART and 'up' turns it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratum is a layer, and so a social level or class.

clue.text: Where movie buffs got bitten by the bug?

definitions.text: Where movie buffs got bitten by the bug?

parts.words: Where movie buffs got bitten by the bug?
parts.note: film fans caught the cinema bug, but in a shabby cinema they were literally bitten by insects

explanation.definitionFit: A grubby old picture house is jokingly said to be infested with insects, hence this name for it.

clue.text: Wino shot back, with resistance halved

indicators.note: the two resistance letters are halved, so one of them goes
back says the word for a shot is read in reverse

parts.note: a report is the bang of a gunshot
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A drunk fires in return, his opposition cut by half.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is a habitual heavy drinker.

clue.text: Hardy sailor's ruled out crossing

indicators.note: the rearranged letters cross over the sailor, enclosing him
out signals the letters are put out of order

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: Captain Hardy, Nelson's sailor, is excluded from crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like Nelson's flag captain; it is the definition. 'out' makes DURLE of 'ruled', with AB inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something durable is tough and long-lasting, as a hardy plant is.

clue.text: Wellington possibly brought about soldier's first advance

indicators.note: the boot is brought about, put around, the letter

parts.note: a wellington is one kind of boot

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The Duke of Wellington may have caused the soldier's first promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wellington' reads as the duke; it is the rubber boot.
explanation.definitionFit: To boost is to push forward or promote, to advance.

clue.text: Are trousers somewhat old-fashioned?

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A fashion query: are these trousers a bit dated?
explanation.definitionFit: Retro styles deliberately imitate fashions of the past.

clue.text: Delicacy of small bird reflected in pure flying

indicators.note: the reversed pair goes in the rearranged letters
flying letters are scattered into a new order
reflected says the words are read backwards, as in a mirror

parts.note: a tit is a small bird

explanation.surface: A delicacy made from a little bird, mirrored in a pure flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' looks like a link joining definition to wordplay, but it is reversed along with the bird; 'flying' rearranges 'pure' to PEUR around them.
explanation.definitionFit: These small fancy cakes or biscuits served after a meal are a sweet treat.

clue.text: Was candidate for diploma beaten ultimately?

indicators.note: ultimately takes the last letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: Did an exam candidate fail to get the certificate in the end?
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stood for election is said to have run for office.

clue.text: In two minds, almost fell

indicators.note: almost means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: someone torn is undecided, in two minds

explanation.surface: Undecided, someone nearly tumbled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' looks like a verb; it is the noun for a hill in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A fell is a hill or moor and a tor is a rocky hilltop.

clue.text: PM formerly a member not going around in county town

parts.note: Lord North was British Prime Minister during the American Revolution
MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: going around says the word turns about, read backwards

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister and an MP avoid travelling round a provincial capital.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the administrative centre of the English county bearing its name, a county town.
